newsitem.title: USA: Contoversy may delay U.S. abortion pill.
newsitem.headline: Contoversy may delay U.S. abortion pill.

text.p: A legal dispute that has erupted over the U.S. license for the French abortion pill RU-486 could delay the introduction of the controversial pill in the United States, its U.S. patentholder said on Friday.
Businessman Joseph Pike, who bought the U.S. license to the pill, was accused in a lawsuit filed by KCC Delaware in Los Angeles on Thursday of using the venture as an illegal money-making scheme.

The New York-based Population Council, which holds U.S. patent rights to the abortion-inducing drug mifepristone and sublicensed them to Pike's companies, said it has asked him to sell his controlling interests.
"Mr. Pike is not an appropriate person to be involved in the introduction of mifepristone in the United States," the council said in a statement.
KCC said it invested $6 million in a company controlled by Pike under the assumption it would own 26 percent of a firm that would manufacture and distribute the drug.

A subsidiary of Beverly Hills, California-based Giant Group Ltd., KCC claimed Pike sold similar stakes to other investors and tried to sell equity interests that combined would total more than 100 percent.
These developments "could delay" the drug's debut into the U.S. market, said council spokeswoman Sandra Waldman.
"We just don't know yet, but it could just hold things up so that the plans can't proceed," she said.
The council said it gave Pike a deadline of a number of days to sell his interests independent of the lawsuit after learning certain information about him in July and negotiating for three months.
KCC said it learned Pike was a disbarred attorney who had pled guilty to forgery in a fraudulent real estate scheme and had been given a two-year suspended prison sentence.
Despite the legal controversy, the Population Council said: "This project will go forward. The individuals to whom we entrust this essential role must exhibit the highest standards of integrity."

The French company Roussel Uclaf, a unit of Hoechst AG, donated the U.S. patent rights for the drug to the council, which set up a company called Advances in Health Technology Inc. in Washington to market it.
But because of anti-abortion sentiment in the United States and violence at abortion clinics, the name of the American manufacturer and distributer had been kept a secret.

The lawsuit said Pike was the principal of San Diego-based Neogen Investors LP and a group of affiliated companies, including Danco Laboratories Inc., which holds the U.S. license for mifepristone as an abortion-inducing drug, and Neogen Pharmaceuticals Inc., which holds the license for all the drug's other potential medical uses.
A spokeswoman for Neogen said Friday that Pike is in the process of sellig his stake in companies but that they do not expect any delay in their plans to manufacture the abortion pill to the U.S.

"We are not thrilled by the lawsuit but it in no way inhibits our plans," said Neogen spokeswoman Leslie Sebastian. "Mr Pike did a very good job of bringing investors together, but there were never any plans to have him on the management team." The Food and Drug Administration recently ruled the drug, which has been used for years throughout much of Europe, was safe and effective. It was expected to approve it for use in the U.S. sometime next year.
